messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Many switched alleles - best way to deal with problem markers?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Many switched alleles - best way to deal with problem markers?
messages.body_plain:
Dr. Broman,

I am having a similar problem on my RIL population consisting of 106 individuals and around 3100 SNPs. I am trying to build a linkage map but I am getting many switched alleles.

I identified multiple linkage groups that were pulling towards each other with the pairwise rf and LOD heatmap (heatmap1) and figured out for a small subset (10-20) of markers per group which linked group had a higher than .5 rf value. When I switched the coding for the markers on those chromosomes, re-ran est.rf() and revisualized the pairwise rf and LOD heatmap it seemed what I did made everything worse (heatmap2). Is there anything that I could do to fix this erroneous coding?

I do have sequencing data for my 2 founder lines. How would I go about checking that the coding is correct?

Thanks a bunch
Rob

On Wednesday, January 23, 2019 at 3:01:15 PM UTC-5 kbr...@gmail.com wrote:
> Do you have data on the founder lines? I would go back to that, because if the genotypes are coded correctly, this problem shouldn't occur. And so I think the most efficient solution would be to identify the cause and fix that.
>
> karl
>
> On 1/23/19 1:55 PM, sjswu...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I'm attempting to build a genetic map for an F2 cross of 127 individuals with approx. 3600 markers across 21 chromosomes and 82 scaffolds (summary attached). I know how many markers I have on each chromosome and scaffold and I've been working through the R/qtl book while cross-referencing with the updated tutorial on genetic map construction online.
> >
> > When I use est.rf() to look at pairwise marker linkages for switched alleles, I get a lengthy list of markers to look at, which I looked at in more detail with checkAlleles() (attached). I can get a better chromosome look at the markers I should investigate with pull.map() but I'm wondering if there is a better/more efficient way of assessing the potential of switched alleles than going marker-by-marker with geno.crosstab()?
> >
> > Any feedback or advice would be appreciated.
> >
> > Thank you!
> >
> > Sara

messages.body_plain:
To me, heatmap 2 is not worse than heatmap 1. Rather, it looks like in the second case, there are a number of sets of linkage groups that should be merged (for example, 14 and 19, 15 and 28, 18 and 27, 20 and 26, 21 and 24, 22 and 25).

The ideal thing is to look at the genotypes of the two parents. You want to code the RILs not as like A,C,G,T, but rather as A for the first parent and B for the second parent. The sequence data for the founder lines should indicate which alleles are which.

karl

Hey Karl,

Sorry to be a bother again. I spent some time looking into identifying the genotypes and alleles from the founder lines and I am unsure how to approach it and I've exhausted people I could ask. I generated my RIL genotype data using ddRADseq and the stacks pipeline. I aligned the reads to a draft scaffold-level genome we have and used the ref.map command. I've looked through my output files and I cannot figure out where the genotype data for the founder lines would be.

Another approach I took was to use the markerlrt() command. It actually generated 26 LG as expected right away. I've been following your tutorial and once again when I got to the pairwise rf and LOD heatmap it was skewed but with the upper left of the plot all yellow (picture attached). Is this usual for markerlrt() command?

As you could see below I checked the summary of the map and I had extremely long group lengths. I noticed that the ave. spacing and max spacing were both 10 so I figured it was by default that the lengths were this long. I started ordering the markers with the orderMarkers() commands and in most cases it would drop the group length to a more reasonable length but in other cases it would still result in groups that were around 800 in length. After looking at the groups that were too long with pull.map() I noticed that it was usually a small group (<30) of markers per group that were causing a huge gap (they were clustered together around 700cM away from the other group of markers). I've been going through each group and systematically removed those markers and each group is actually shaping up into acceptable lengths. I guess this was a long-winded way of asking whether or not this approach is viable and is producing an accurate linkage map? Could these problem markers actually be added back later? It is my idea that these markers might the ones with their alleles switched but I am not sure. Thanks a bunch for any help or advice you may have.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Many switched alleles - best way to deal with problem markers?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Many switched alleles - best way to deal with problem markers?
messages.body_plain:
Figuring out the parental genotypes will be crucial to making a linkage map with R/qtl. It's also crucial for QTL mapping in R/qtl, in the method for handling missing genotypes and to do interval mapping. Even if you were to resort to association analysis, it would be good to know the founder origin of the alleles, to understand the direction of QTL effects. Generally, I would recommend genotyping the founders alongside the RIL.

markerlrt just does the equivalent of a chi-square test for association for each marker pair. It will help to find linkage groups, but to go beyond that to order the markers within a linkage group, you'll still need to deal with the marker phase issue.

One approach you could take would be to make a second version of all of the markers with the phase swapped. Form those into linkage groups using est.rf(), and you should get two copies of each linkage group, one with each phase. So then drop one from each of the pairs of linkage groups.

The plot of the markerlrt results seems messed up; it's supposed to give a symmetric plot, as there are no estimates of recombination fractions. Using what="lod" in plotRF() should give you the right plot, but there's supposed to be an attribute in the output that indicates that there are no rf estimates.

Finally, the initial map after forming linkage groups has all markers placed an arbitrary 10 cM apart, so that's why use see both average spacing and maximum spacing being 10. can only have max == ave if the values are all identical.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr.Broman,

What do you suggest in situations when LOD score is high after running ripple but the chromosome length also increases? I am particularly concerned when chromosome length increases by more than 1 centiMorgan. Please find the screenshot of one of my example codes' attached.

Thank you.

On Monday, November 30, 2020 at 12:35:07 PM UTC-6 Pummi Singh wrote:
> Great. Thank you Dr.Broman.
>
> On Mon, Nov 30, 2020 at 12:30 PM Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > If you use the likelihood method in ripple(), it will re-estimate inter-marker distances with each marker order, using an iterative algorithm. The warning message is issued if that algorithm doesn't converge. You can increase the maxit argument to try to achieve convergence, but it probably doesn't matter and can be ignored, as the lack of convergence is mostly happening for marker orders with lower support.
> >
> > The LOD scores are log10 likelihood relative to the initial order, so yes the one with the largest value is preferred. See the help file for ripple(): "the last two columns are LOD scores (log base 10 likelihood ratios) comparing each order to the initial order and the estimated chromosome length for the given order. Positive LOD scores indicate that the alternate order has more support than the original."
> >
> > karl
> >
> > On Monday, November 30, 2020 at 12:16:54 PM UTC-6 pummi...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Hi Dr.Broman,
> > >
> > > I had a quick question about ripple function. Please find the document attached. In the first screenshot, certain orders do not converge (shown as "Didn't converge!" in red). I was wondering if that is a problem that needs attention.
> > >
> > > In the second screenshot, different orders of the markers with LOD scores are present. messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] R/QTL for biparental population
messages.body_plain:
Without any other information about physical order of the markers, I'd go with the order with highest likelihood, even if the estimated chromosome length increases slightly.

karl

> > On Mon, Nov 30, 2020 at 12:30 PM Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > If you use the likelihood method in ripple(), it will re-estimate inter-marker distances with each marker order, using an iterative algorithm. The warning message is issued if that algorithm doesn't converge. You can increase the maxit argument to try to achieve convergence, but it probably doesn't matter and can be ignored, as the lack of convergence is mostly happening for marker orders with lower support.
> > >
> > > The LOD scores are log10 likelihood relative to the initial order, so yes the one with the largest value is preferred. See the help file for ripple(): "the last two columns are LOD scores (log base 10 likelihood ratios) comparing each order to the initial order and the estimated chromosome length for the given order. Positive LOD scores indicate that the alternate order has more support than the original."

The warning message is issued if that algorithm doesn't converge. You can increase the maxit argument to try to achieve convergence, but it probably doesn't matter and can be ignored, as the lack of convergence is mostly happening for marker orders with lower support.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The LOD scores are log10 likelihood relative to the initial order, so yes the one with the largest value is preferred. See the help file for ripple(): "the last two columns are LOD scores (log base 10 likelihood ratios) comparing each order to the initial order and the estimated chromosome length for the given order. messages.body_plain:
I was thinking that you'd drop the chromosomes with subset(), or get around those chromosomes when you try to pull the log likelihood values.

Since the problem is that sapply( ) is returning a list, due to some chromosomes returning NULL, you could change that line to have unlist(lapply(  )), as that will strip of the NULL values:

    sum(unlist(lapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik")))

karl

PS It would be a bit easier to respond/work with your code if you copy-pasted it into your message rather than adding a screen shot image.

> > > > > > > > > > If you use the likelihood method in ripple(), it will re-estimate inter-marker distances with each marker order, using an iterative algorithm. The warning message is issued if that algorithm doesn't converge. You can increase the maxit argument to try to achieve convergence, but it probably doesn't matter and can be ignored, as the lack of convergence is mostly happening for marker orders with lower support.
> > > > > > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Dr.Broman. Sorry about the screenshots. I will make sure that I have the code and error pasted instead.

On Tue, Dec 8, 2020 at 10:18 AM Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I was thinking that you'd drop the chromosomes with subset(), or get around those chromosomes when you try to pull the log likelihood values.
>
> Since the problem is that sapply( ) is returning a list, due to some chromosomes returning NULL, you could change that line to have unlist(lapply(  )), as that will strip of the NULL values:
>
>     sum(unlist(lapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik")))
>
> karl
>
> PS It would be a bit easier to respond/work with your code if you copy-pasted it into your message rather than adding a screen shot image.
>
> On Tuesday, December 8, 2020 at 10:03:07 AM UTC-6 pummi...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Does that mean dropping the markers associated with these groups?
> >
> > Thanks
> >
> > On Monday, December 7, 2020 at 10:50:23 PM UTC-6 kbr...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > Drop the groups with just one marker. They don't have a log likelihood and so are messing things up.
> > >
> > > karl
> > >
> > > On Mon, Dec 7, 2020 at 10:27 PM Pummi Singh <pummi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi Dr.Broman,
> > > >
> > > > Attached are the results that I got. I have 17 linkage groups of which groups 15 to 17 have a single marker each. I apologize for several questions, I am very new to R.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks
> > > >
> > > > On Monday, December 7, 2020 at 10:09:15 PM UTC-6 kbr...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > I would pull it apart and try to figure out what's going wrong.
> > > > > Look at the output of sapply(tempmap, attr, "loglik") which should be a vector of log likelihood values.
> > > > >
> > > > > karl
> > > > >
> > > > > On Monday, December 7, 2020 at 9:55:48 PM UTC-6 pummi...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > I am attaching a word doc with the code and error because I am not sure if what I pasted is visible or not.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks
> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Monday, December 7, 2020 at 9:47:52 PM UTC-6 Pummi Singh wrote:

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I am getting the following error while running the code for estimating genotyping error rate. Please let me know how to fix this.

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > On Monday, December 7, 2020 at 9:32:57 AM UTC-6 kbr...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > Without any other information about physical order of the markers, I'd go with the order with highest likelihood, even if the estimated chromosome length increases slightly.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > karl
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On Sunday, December 6, 2020 at 12:45:06 PM UTC-6 pummi...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hi Dr.Broman,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > What do you suggest in situations when LOD score is high after running ripple but the chromosome length also increases? I am particularly concerned when chromosome length increases by more than 1 centiMorgan. Please find the screenshot of one of my example codes' attached.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thank you.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Monday, November 30, 2020 at 12:35:07 PM UTC-6 Pummi Singh wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > Great. Thank you Dr.Broman.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > On Mon, Nov 30, 2020 at 12:30 PM Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > If you use the likelihood method in ripple(), it will re-estimate inter-marker distances with each marker order, using an iterative algorithm. The warning message is issued if that algorithm doesn't converge. You can increase the maxit argument to try to achieve convergence, but it probably doesn't matter and can be ignored, as the lack of convergence is mostly happening for marker orders with lower support.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > The LOD scores are log10 likelihood relative to the initial order, so yes the one with the largest value is preferred. See the help file for ripple(): "the last two columns are LOD scores (log base 10 likelihood ratios) comparing each order to the initial order and the estimated chromosome length for the given order. Positive LOD scores indicate that the alternate order has more support than the original."
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > karl
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Monday, November 30, 2020 at 12:16:54 PM UTC-6 pummi...@gmail.com wrote:

> > > > > > > > > > > > In the second screenshot, different orders of the markers with LOD scores are present. It is my understanding that Order 1 is preferred over the Initial (also the rest of them) because of high LOD and lower chromosome length. Also, it appears that every consecutive order of markers is presented such that LODs are in decreasing order (because I am not able to see what data is in those 12 additional rows). Please let me know if this is true.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

To add onto this, as suggested in a previous discussion. I started with the physical positions, assuming these are correct (converting the physical position to cM by dividing by 1,000,000).

I am working with maternal markers (backcross, AB x AA) from an outbred population.  I see significantly inflated estimates of map sizes.  So far, I have gone through several iterations of rippling using increases window sizes (3,4,5, etc.) and at each window, repeat the cycle until no new XOs are identified with that window size before moving up.  I am seeing incremental changes but still have significantly inflated map sizes.

I'm wondering if there is a way to format the for loop to iterate over a list of increasing window sizes and then move onto a new window size when no improvements are found? Additionally, would there be a way to record how many iterations were needed at each window size interval (i.e. append the results from each iteration to a file that was stored separately from the ripple results)?

I've adapted the code from the book (pgs.60-66) and have it included here:

rip <- vector("list", nchr(fake.qtl))
names(rip) <- names(fake.qtl$geno)

for ( i in names(fake.qtl$geno))
  rip[[i]] <- ripple(fake.qtl, i, 7, method = "countxo")

dif.nxo <- sapply(rip, function(a) a[1, ncol(a)] - a[2,ncol(a)])
dif.nxo

for ( i in names(fake.qtl$geno)) {
  if(dif.nxo[i] > 0)
    fake.qtl <- switch.order(fake.qtl, i, rip[[i]][2,])
}

It would greatly help to automate this process and also be able to review the output after the fact to identify areas that were potentially problematic for ordering, etc.

Thanks,
Josh

Hi Dr.Broman,

I deleted a marker thinking that it might improve my results but that did not happen. I want to insert that marker back on its linkage group. I have so far not been successful at findin

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] R/QTL for biparental population
messages.body_plain:
There's not a way to put it back if you've deleted it from the cross. Rather than delete markers, I would move them to some "unlinked" linkage group or chromosome. To get the data back, you'll need to go back to the original data set.

karl

> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > The LOD scores are log10 likelihood relative to the initial order, so yes the one with the largest value is preferred. > > > > > > > > > > > > > > If you use the likelihood method in ripple(), it will re-estimate inter-marker distances with each marker order, using an iterative algorithm. The warning message is issued if that algorithm doesn't converge. You can increase the maxit argument to try to achieve convergence, but it probably doesn't matter and can be ignored, as the lack of convergence is mostly happening for marker orders with lower support.
> > > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > > The LOD scores are log10 likelihood relative to the initial order, so yes the one with the largest value is preferred. See the help file for ripple(): "the last two columns are LOD scores (log base 10 likelihood ratios) comparing each order to the initial order and the estimated chromosome length for the given order. Positive LOD scores indicate that the alternate order has more support than the original."

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr.Broman,

I had to move certain markers from one linkage group to another and as a result, the first marker of the initial linkage group starts from a number other than 0 cM. I am not sure if this is fine. Please let me know if there is some way to fix this. An example is attached. I had to move the markers highlighted in orange to another linkage group. After moving the markers, I ran the following for the linkage group to and from which markers were moved.

```{r}
genmap <- orderMarkers(genmap, chr=2)
pull.map(genmap, chr=2)
```
```{r}
rip2 <- ripple(genmap, chr=2, window=7)
summary(rip2)
```
```{r}
rip2lik <- ripple(genmap, chr=2, window=4, method="likelihood", error.prob=0.005)
summary(rip2lik)
```
I also used switch.order after ripple based on LOD values.

Please let me know.

Thanks

Pummi

messages.body_plain:
There's a function shiftmap() that can be used to shift all chromosomes so they start at 0.

karl

On Tuesday, December 15, 2020 at 9:59:24 PM UTC-6 pummi...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Dr.Broman,
>
> I had to move certain markers from one linkage group to another and as a result, the first marker of the initial linkage group starts from a number other than 0 cM. I am not sure if this is fine. Please let me know if there is some way to fix this. An example is attached. I had to move the markers highlighted in orange to another linkage group. After moving the markers, I ran the following for the linkage group to and from which markers were moved.
>
> ```{r}
> genmap <- orderMarkers(genmap, chr=2)
> pull.map(genmap, chr=2)
> ```
> ```{r}
> rip2 <- ripple(genmap, chr=2, window=7)
> summary(rip2)
> ```
> ```{r}
> rip2lik <- ripple(genmap, chr=2, window=4, method="likelihood", error.prob=0.005)
> summary(rip2lik)
> ```
> I also used switch.order after ripple based on LOD values.
>
> Please let me know.
>
> Thanks
>
> Pummi

>

Thank you

Pummi

I am not sure if this is fine. Please let me know if there is some way to fix this. An example is attached. I had to move the markers highlighted in orange to another linkage group. After moving the markers, I ran the following for the linkage group to and from which markers were moved.
> > >
> > > ```{r}
> > > genmap <- orderMarkers(genmap, chr=2)
> > > pull.map(genmap, chr=2)
> > > ```
> > > ```{r}
> > > rip2 <- ripple(genmap, chr=2, window=7)
> > > summary(rip2)
> > > ```
> > > ```{r}
> > > rip2lik <- ripple(genmap, chr=2, window=4, method="likelihood", error.prob=0.005)
> > > summary(rip2lik)
> > > ```
> > > I also used switch.order after ripple based on LOD values.
> > >
> > > Please let me know.
> > >
> > > Thanks

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] R/QTL for biparental population
messages.body_plain:
First pull out the map and get the lengths of the linkage groups. I'll use the cross 'fake.bc' as an example.

  library(qtl)
  data(fake.bc)
  map <- pull.map(fake.bc)
  L <- sapply(map, function(chr) diff(range(chr)))

Then reorder the chromosomes by reordering the components of the "geno" part of the cross.

  fake.bc$geno <- fake.bc$geno[order(L, decreasing=TRUE)]

If you want to change the names of the groups, you can change the names of the "geno" part of the cross

  names(fake.bc$geno) <- 1:nchr(fake.bc)

karl

Thanks so much Dr.Broman.

On Wed, Dec 23, 2020 at 8:42 AM Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> First pull out the map and get the lengths of the linkage groups. I'll use the cross 'fake.bc' as an example.
>
>   library(qtl)
>   data(fake.bc)
>   map <- pull.map(fake.bc)
>   L <- sapply(map, function(chr) diff(range(chr)))
>
> Then reorder the chromosomes by reordering the components of the "geno" part of the cross.
>
>   fake.bc$geno <- fake.bc$geno[order(L, decreasing=TRUE)]
>
> If you want to change the names of the groups, you can change the names of the "geno" part of the cross
>
>   names(fake.bc$geno) <- 1:nchr(fake.bc)
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr. Broman
I want to calculate multiple qtl analysis while considering covariate and interaction covariate .in the scanone analysis for example I used this script

QTL_hk2<-scanone(QTL__root_length_TREATMENT_1, pheno.col=2,method="hk",addcovar = RL_C,intcovar= RL_C )
 and the results showed strong evidence of one qtl on chr=5

for multiple qtl analysis   I used below scripts:

M_QTL<- calc.genoprob(QTL_root_length_TREATMENT, step=1)

M_qtl <- makeqtl(M_QTL, chr=c( "1","5"), pos=c(19, 53), what="prob")

summary(M_qtl)

out.fq <- fitqtl(QTL__root_length_TREATMENT, qtl=M_qtl,pheno.col=2, method="hk",formula=y~Q1+Q2)
summary(out.fq)

summary(fitqtl(QTL_root_length_TREATMENT, qtl=M_qtl, pheno.col=2, method="hk", get.ests=TRUE, dropone=FALSE))

covar <- data.frame(RL_C=QTL__root_length_TREATMENT$pheno$RL_C)

addcovarint(QTL_root_length_TREATMENT, pheno.col=2,M_qtl, covar,"RL_C" , formula=y~Q1+Q2, method="hk" )

But the result was weird, they didn't show any significant qtl .

My question is : am I used  the correct way to add covariate and interacting covariate in multiple qtl analysis ?
Is there any other function for calculate multiple qtl with covariate and interacting covariate ?
Thank you in advance
Zahra PAKBAZ

messages.body_plain:
In what way was the result weird?

You can investigate interactive covariates in fitqtl() by comparing results with different formulas. That's what addcovarint() does: it adds a QTL x covariate interaction and compares the fit of the model with and without that interaction.

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] calculate multiple qtl with covariate and interacting covariate
messages.body_plain:
The LOD scores from addcovarint() are for tests of the QTL x covariate interaction. In scanone, you'd take the difference between the LOD score with RL_C as interactive covariate and the LOD score when it is just an additive covariate. That the LOD score for the QTL x covariate interaction is small suggests that there is no evidence for the QTL effect being modified by RL_C value.

karl

Hello Karl

I've used R/qtl for ages and have yet to come across this problem:

Syn<-read.cross("csvs",dir="",genotypes=c("AA","BB"),alleles=c("A","B"),genfile="geno.csv",phefile= "pheno.csv", na.strings="NA",".")

Can you please suggest what I can do to fix the genotype % and Observed genotypes errors?

Thanks so much,
Annie

messages.subject: Re: Incorrect Genotype %
messages.body_plain:
The code you sent with the file is somewhat different than what you typed above.

Syn<-read.cross("csvs",dir="",genotypes=c("AA","AB","BB"),alleles=c("A","B"),genfile="geno.csv",phefile= "pheno.csv", na.strings="NA",".")

class(Syn)[1] <-"riself"

summary(Syn)

I think the problem is that there are some heterozygous genotypes in there, so it would be read in as an intercross with genotypes converted to numbers 1,2,3, but then when you convert to riself you end up only using the 1,2 genotypes so the het genotypes are assumed to be BB.

Rather than changing the cross type with class(Syn)[1] <- "riself", it is best to use the function convert2riself().
Alternatively, include crosstype="riself" in the call to read.cross().

Also, the bit at the end of the read.cross() command leaves "." hanging. You want na.strings=c("NA", ".")

I would read in these data with:

    Syn<-read.cross("csv",dir="",genotypes=c("AA","BB"),alleles=c("A","B"),file="geno.csv", na.strings=c("AB","NA","."), crosstype="riself")

karl

Hi Karl,

As per the previous conversation, I would like to develop the foreach loop to iterate through each chromosome using increasingly larger window sizes.  It produces the following error: Error in switch.order(fake.qtl, i, rip[[i]][2, ]) : Chr 5221 not found.

Josh

library(foreach)
library(qtl)

fake.qtl <- read.cross("csv", file = "/path/to/file.csv", estimate.map = TRUE, genotypes = c("A", "H"), na.strings = c("-", "NA"))
summary(fake.qtl)
todrop <- rownames(gt[gt$P.value < 1e-4,])
fake.qtl <- drop.markers(fake.qtl, todrop)

rip <- vector("list", nchr(fake.qtl))
names(rip) <- names(fake.qtl$geno)

dif.nxo <- sapply(rip, function(a) a[1, ncol(a)] - a[2,ncol(a)])

foreach( i = names(fake.qtl$geno), b = 2:5) %do%
  rip[[i]] <- ripple(fake.qtl, i, b, method = "countxo") %:% when (dif.nxo > 0) %do%

  fake.qtl <- switch.order(fake.qtl, i, rip[[i]][2,])
